Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: satisfied because the paper concretely analyzes rule-type mechanisms directly governing settlement-level drinking-water access, including (1) statutory population-size eligibility screening under National Law No. 10.988/10.998 (>3,000 inhabitants plus hygiene exceptions, under which Villa Dolores qualified whereas neighboring San Pedro applied despite failing the population requirement and remained unserved), (2) tariff and cost-recovery reform under National Law No. 12.140 (1935) reducing water tariffs so financially constrained municipalities could join OSN without prohibitive tariffs, (3) utility ownership structure and expropriation (provincial expropriation of private waterworks in Mina Clavero in 1929 and transfer of municipal systems to federal public enterprise OSN; provincial DGH regulation under Cordoba Law No. 3732 and Decree No. 26.819), and (4) intergovernmental contracting/administrative rules (bilateral convenios requiring provincial legislative ratification, shared land expropriation resolved by municipal referendum, and public-domain water allocation rules overriding municipal monopoly claims against Cura Brochero).
rationale: Archival environmental-history case study examining drinking-water access across settlements in Argentina's southern Gran Chaco (1930-1960). Although framed broadly around hydrosocial modernization, it empirically analyzes concrete rule-type legal, ownership, eligibility and tariff mechanisms governing service access at the settlement/municipality level — specifically statutory population-size eligibility cutoffs (>3,000 inhabitants under Law No. 10.988/10.998, excluding smaller applicants such as San Pedro), tariff-reduction rules (Law No. 12.140 overcoming prohibitive municipal cost-recovery tariffs), expropriation of private waterworks, municipal-to-federal utility transfers to OSN via legislatively ratified convenios, and public-domain water-allocation rulings — alongside primary archival and census evidence on piped water coverage (~80% of regional urban population) and persistent rural/lowland exclusion. Eligible in Spanish under Criterion 10 as full-text translation is feasible.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, this study WOULD satisfy Criterion 2 in isolation because it discusses municipal water and environmental governance institutions and policies (including the 1994 Shenzhen SEZ Water Resources Administration Regulations, sewage fee adjustments, the PPP joint venture with Veolia and subsequent re-nationalization of Shenzhen Water Group, and the River Chief System); however, the overall plain_criterion2_decision is still 'exclude' because Criteria 1 and 4 fail. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is 'no': these governance reforms and utility ownership shifts are analyzed only as macro state-capital-nature processes driving commodification, de-commodification, river ecological restoration, and waterfront spatial transformation, not as rule-type mechanisms directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access.
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic). Based on the full Chinese text and English abstract, this urban political ecology case study traces 40+ years of macro city-water ('waterscape') transformation, river/marine water pollution remediation, and public waterfront greenway ('blue belt' / 碧道) construction in Shenzhen. Although it mentions municipal water institutions, sewage fees, and the PPP-to-state-owned restructuring of Shenzhen Water Group as part of its macro state-capital-nature narrative, it does not examine household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access, connections, reliability, affordability, or exclusion, and 'public access' in the third phase refers solely to public recreational/ecological waterfront spaces. Under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain broad reading of Criterion 2, the study is excluded because Criteria 1 and 4 are not met.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Passes the plain/literal wording of Criterion 2 because it examines participatory planning governance in slum settlement upgrading (evaluated via Arnstein's Ladder of Citizen Participation and benchmarked against Law No. 25 of 2004, Government Regulation No. 68 of 2010, and PUPR Ministerial Regulation No. 14 of 2018). Fails the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2 because it focuses on generic community participation in landscape and slum-upgrading project planning and cites sectoral regulations only as normative physical standards, without examining any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation requirements for connection, tariff rules, enforcement, discretion, or utility regulatory structure) directly governing household water or sanitation service access. Land tenure disputes are mentioned only briefly in relation to public open space development, not water or sanitation access.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification of Criterion 2. Although the study collects primary empirical data reporting household drinking water (PDAM and well use, monthly water spending) and sanitation/wastewater conditions in an urban kampong in Bogor, Indonesia, its governance analysis focuses solely on general community participation in neighborhood slum-upgrading and landscape planning (using Arnstein's Ladder) and cites national housing/water regulations only as descriptive physical benchmarks. It does not examine any legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or utility governance structure) directly governing water or sanitation service access. Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included as an empirical study examining participatory planning governance alongside slum water and sanitation conditions.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper does examine legal, administrative, and governance factors in urban land management (such as Market Value Analysis zoning, the Detroit Future City planning framework, the unimplemented 1999 Michigan Urban Homestead Act, and municipal disposition of tax-foreclosed parcels), though these concern land redevelopment rather than water or sanitation services. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, Criterion 2 is 'no' because the paper does not analyze any rule-type mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access (such as utility eligibility rules, documentation/tenure requirements for water connection, tariffs, disconnection enforcement, or water utility governance). Under both the plain and narrow readings of Criterion 2, the overall screening decision is exclude because Criteria 1 and 4 are not met.
rationale: Excluded under E01 (Wrong topic). While this is an empirical qualitative political-ecology study in Detroit, its subject is postindustrial vacant land governance, settler colonial property logics, urban greening, and the Hantz Woodlands urban tree farm. Water and sewage are mentioned only in passing as part of bundled municipal services slated for potential long-term withdrawal in high-vacancy zones, with no empirical analysis of water or sanitation service access (failing c1), no rule-type mechanism governing water/sanitation access (failing narrow c2), and no water or sanitation access outcomes reported (failing c4).

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: PASSES PLAIN WORDING / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 RULE-TYPE READING. Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study examines institutional and governance factors in Chennai's sanitation sector via a Social Network Analysis of municipal and state agencies (GCC, CMWSSB, TNSCB), expert-identified governance barriers to non-sewered sanitation uptake (poor inter-agency coordination, lack of political will, weak monitoring/accountability and effluent quality enforcement, systemic corruption, and a 2006 building mandate for decentralized treatment in >20,000 sqm residential buildings), and institutional planning criteria (level of decentralised management, O&M demands, user awareness); however, even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the overall study decision remains exclude because Criteria 4 and 5 fail (no empirical household/community service-access outcome is analysed in relation to those factors). Under the active narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is 'no': the study develops a multi-criteria technology-planning catalogue and maps broad stakeholder networks and macro-governance/implementation barriers rather than empirically examining a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household or community service access. Passing descriptive mentions of CMWSSB's 'Azhaithal Inaippu' 10-instalment sewer connection fee scheme (p. 6) and the Manual Scavenging Act 2011 debate over container-based sanitation (p. 5) are unanalysed background context.
rationale: Excluded (E03 - Wrong exposure; also fails C4/C5 on access outcome). This mixed-methods study formulates and weights a 14-criteria decision-aiding catalogue (physical, technical, institutional, and financial indicators) for municipal planners to select between sewered and non-sewered sanitation technologies in Chennai, supplemented by a citywide Faecal Waste Flow Diagram (SFD) update, stakeholder Social Network Analysis, and expert-identified drivers/barriers to scaling non-sewered sanitation. Under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, it does not empirically examine any legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism governing household or community service access (a two-sentence background mention of CMWSSB's 'Azhaithal Inaippu' 10-instalment sewer connection fee scheme on p. 6 is purely descriptive context). Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2—which the study's institutional stakeholder mapping and governance barrier analysis would satisfy—the paper remains excluded because its empirical outcomes are planning-criteria weights, stakeholder centrality, municipal technology-adoption barriers, and theoretical ward technology suitability scores (using assumed ward coverage) rather than household or community service-access outcomes.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Plain wording of Criterion 2: YES — the study examines institutional, administrative, and governance factors in decentralised rural service delivery, including District Council mandates under the Local Government Act of 1998, inter-organisational power relations, and bureaucratic financial accountability rules between local governments and donors/NGOs. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — the factors studied concern inter-organisational project delivery, planning coordination, and donor grant disbursement between NGOs/donors and District Councils rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation or tenure requirements, tariffs or cost-recovery rules, disconnection/enforcement, or utility regulatory structure governing consumer access). Note: even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains exclude because the study fails Criterion 1 and Criterion 4 (no water service access outcome).
rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome; also fails narrow Criterion 2 and Criterion 1). Although situated in Malawi's rural water supply sector, this qualitative cross-case study examines how inter-organisational power and control shape cross-sector partnerships between donors/NGOs and District Councils. Its outcome is strictly organisational—the level of local government involvement in project delivery (little to no involvement, coordinating, partaking, or leading)—with no empirical measurement of household or community water access, availability, reliability, affordability, or exclusion (explicitly deferred to future research on p. 204 / PDF p. 13). In addition, under the 2026-10-13 narrow Criterion 2 reading, the donor-council project planning and fund-disbursement practices examined are inter-organisational project delivery governance rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Passes the plain/literal wording of Criterion 2, but FAILS the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper discusses municipal governance collapse, provincial financial administration, intergovernmental interventions (DWS, Rand Water, ERWAT, SANDF), the SAHRC inquiry, High Court public-meeting orders, and Section 63 of the Water Services Act of 1997. Under the 2026-10-13 clarification, however, the paper does NOT examine a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing household/community service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility/regulatory structure governing access); instead, it narrates generic WWTW maintenance/upgrade project delivery delays, capital funding shortfalls, contractor work stoppages, and macro-governance background. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' because the paper fails c1, c4, and c5.
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic): Tempelhoff (2021) is an environmental and urban history of the Vaal River Barrage sub-catchment (1891-2021) examining raw sewage pollution, fish kills, and the operational collapse of Emfuleni Local Municipality's bulk wastewater treatment works rather than household or community water/sanitation service access (which appears only tangentially in historical/descriptive passages). It also fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading because it chronicles generic WWTW maintenance/upgrade delays, capital funding shortfalls, contractor protests, and macro-governance decay rather than a rule-type mechanism governing service access, and fails Criterion 5 because it is an unstructured historical narrative without a reported empirical study design or identifiable service-access population-exposure-outcome framework (so plain_criterion2_decision is also 'exclude').

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is not met (no): the study's primary exposure is hydrological/physical water delivery (absolute weekly flow, flow percentile relative to peers, and self-reported 5-year flow decline) as a driver of farmer perceptions, rather than a rule-type mechanism governing service access. Although the regressions include CWP-level institutional control variables that reflect rule-type features (conditions to join such as land ownership, membership fees, and chief authorization; cost to become a member; annual cost of membership; and number of monitoring groups), the paper never examines how those rules govern or affect water service access, connection, or flow—they are entered solely as controls in models of drought perception and subjective satisfaction. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the inclusion of CWP governance and institutional controls touches on institutional/governance factors (so plain Criterion 2 alone could be read as satisfied), but plain_criterion2_decision is still exclude because the study fails Criterion 4 (no water access outcome).
rationale: Excluded primarily for wrong outcome (E04), as well as lacking an analysis of rule-type mechanisms governing service access under Criterion 2. Rather than modeling water service access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion as an outcome, this study of small-scale irrigation Community Water Projects (CWPs) in Kenya treats household piped water flow (absolute flow, flow relative to peers, and flow relative to past levels) as the primary hydrological predictor—alongside CWP institutional controls (joining fees, annual costs, conditions to join, monitoring groups)—to explain two perceptual/attitudinal outcomes: farmers' agricultural drought risk perceptions and subjective Likert-scale satisfaction with their CWP. No empirical relationship between legal/institutional rules and water access or delivery outcomes is tested, so the study is excluded under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain reading of Criterion 2.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Cannot assess under either the plain wording of Criterion 2 or the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading because the target paper (Whaley & Cleaver, 2017, DOI: 10.1016/j.wrr.2017.04.001) was not retrieved. Both the plain reading and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading therefore yield cannot_tell/unclear until the correct full text is obtained.
rationale: WRONG_PAPER_MISMATCH (paper_mention_mismatch; reason: "full text not accessible" for target record): Record metadata specifies Whaley L. & Cleaver F. (2017), "Can ‘functionality’ save the community management model of rural water supply?", Water Resources and Rural Development (DOI: 10.1016/j.wrr.2017.04.001), whereas the retrieved 15-page PDF is an entirely different article — Nespect Salom & Prudence Khumalo (2022), "Challenges Facing Community Management of Rural Water Supply: The Case of Ohangwena Region, Namibia", African Studies Quarterly 21(1): 28-42 — which merely cites Whaley & Cleaver (2017) in its reference list on PDF Page 14. Per screening rules, guessing from title or outside memory is prohibited, requiring decision = "cannot_tell" and exclusion_code = "NONE".

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study examines legal, institutional and governance factors (Mexico's National Water Law concession regime, the 1957 restricted-access presidential decree, CONAGUA inspection/enforcement gaps, corruption/apocryphal water rights, court injunctions and River Basin Councils). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, although water-rights permitting, restricted-access rules and enforcement are rule-type legal mechanisms, here they govern agricultural irrigation and raw watershed resource extraction rather than household or community water or sanitation service access (so narrow c2 = no). Because Criterion 1 and Criterion 4 fail regardless, the overall full-text decision under both the plain wording and narrow reading of Criterion 2 is exclude.
rationale: Excluded as E07 (Wrong service; Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). This qualitative empirical study investigates adaptive watershed governance, CONAGUA water-rights concessions, corruption and farmer conflicts over agricultural irrigation water and water ecosystem services in the Rio del Carmen watershed, Chihuahua, Mexico. Over 90% of aquifer extraction is for commercial/agricultural crop irrigation (pecans, maize, chilli, cotton, alfalfa, sorghum), and the paper does not examine household or community drinking-water supply or sanitation service access.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper passes Criterion 2 because it examines institutional, statutory, and governance factors in water resources (specifically National Water Act limits on WUA management authority, delays in groundwater use authorizations, national groundwater strategies, and DWS internal bureaucratic culture). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it fails Criterion 2 ('no') because it does not examine a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules, tariffs, disconnections, or utility regulation of household access), focusing instead on common-pool groundwater resource management and macro-organizational public-service culture. Note: plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' because the paper independently fails Criteria 1, 3, 4, and 5.
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; see Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). Seward, Xu, and Turton (2015) apply conceptual backcasting, Ostrom's common-pool resource design principles, government strategy documents, and the lead author's personal career reflections as a hydrogeologist to explore how South Africa's Department of Water and Sanitation (DWS) could improve national groundwater resource governance (e.g., delegating groundwater management to Water User Associations and overcoming bureaucratic dysfunction). The paper does not study household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access (failing c1), does not examine a rule-type mechanism governing service access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification (failing narrow c2, though addressing public-sector water-resource governance under plain c2), lacks systematic primary empirical evidence or a systematic empirical synthesis (failing c3), and reports no service-access outcome (failing c4). Under both the narrow and plain readings of Criterion 2, the study is excluded.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Passes the plain/literal broad wording of Criterion 2 because it examines internal utility administration and 'drinking water supply governance' across PDAM Tirta Kualo's five working units as well as alignment with the Tanjungbalai City spatial plan (2013-2033). However, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2: 'governance' here consists of generic operational, technical, and human-resource issues (leaking pipes, damaged or missing water meters, lack of laboratory testing, low HR capacity, unpaid staff salaries), hydrological supply-demand calculations, and spatial land-use planning. Although Table 2 briefly notes in single diagnostic sentences that the utility is not at full cost recovery and has undetected illegal connections, the paper does not examine any tariff or cost-recovery rule, eligibility or tenure requirement, administrative burden, enforcement policy, or regulatory/ownership rule governing household service access.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. Although titled as a study of 'sustainable drinking water governance' and reporting municipal piped water coverage (68.86%), the empirical analysis consists of raw water capacity and population demand projections, a descriptive inventory of internal operational/technical/HR problems across PDAM Tirta Kualo's five working units (old pipes, broken/missing meters, low HR quality, lack of lab testing), and a normative upgrade model aligned with the municipal spatial plan. It does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, administrative burdens, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or regulatory/ownership structure) governing household service access. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included as a descriptive mixed-methods case study of utility governance and service coverage.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, though borderline in scope breadth. Under the plain wording, the review clearly examines institutional, governance, policy, and regulatory factors (private and social enterprise roles, public-private partnerships, civil society interfaces, decentralisation, and regulation). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, substantial portions of the review cover sanitation marketing, supply-chain viability, and CSO capacity building (which alone would be out-of-scope commercial/behavioural promotion or project delivery), but the review also explicitly synthesizes empirical evidence on multiple rule-type mechanisms directly governing poor households' service access: (1) provider ownership, contracting, and regulatory structures (for-profit private operators vs. social enterprises, rural piped-water PPPs, municipal-utility delegated management models, legalisation/formalisation of informal providers, licensing/taxes, accreditation, neighbourhood regulatory decentralisation, and enforcement fines on illegal dumping); (2) tariff, connection-fee, cost-recovery, and subsidy rules (high connection fees preventing poor households from connecting or locking them in, cost-recovery water tariffs pricing out poor rural households, and hardware/community or output-based connection subsidies); and (3) pricing discretion/accommodation (flexible pricing structures and instalment/credit payment schemes for poor customers).
rationale: This 2014 paper matches the record metadata and is a full-text systematic empirical synthesis (eligible under Criterion 3) examining private and social enterprise roles in water and sanitation services for the poor across low- and lower-middle-income countries. Although a substantial share of the reviewed literature concerns enterprise viability, sanitation marketing, and CSO capacity building, the review explicitly synthesizes empirical evidence on rule-type mechanisms under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification: private/social operator ownership, rural water PPPs, and municipal-utility delegated management models; formalisation, licensing, accreditation, and neighbourhood-level regulation of informal providers; and connection fees, cost-recovery tariffs, flexible/instalment pricing accommodations, and subsidies directly governing poor households' water and sanitation access, affordability, and exclusion. All inclusion criteria (c1-c6) are met for systematic-review inclusion (noting Criterion 6 is a quantitative-synthesis gate, not a review-eligibility gate). Confidence is rated medium because the review blends in-scope ownership, regulatory, and tariff/connection-fee mechanisms with broader sanitation-marketing and supply-chain enterprise themes.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: PASSES PLAIN WORDING (plain C2 = yes) BUT FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 RULE-TYPE READING (narrow C2 = no). Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper examines institutional and governance factors: Section 3.1 ('Governance Factors', category score = 247) interviews ministry, regional/provincial, municipal, and NGO actors regarding institutional pre-triggering with village leaders, NGO-government coordination, national policy ambiguity between subsidized and unsubsidized CLTS implementation, and High Commissioner mediation for ODF certification, while Section 3.5.4 notes informal sanctions/fines threatened by village authorities against holdout households. Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is 'no' because the intervention and determinants studied are behavioural promotion (CLTS social-norm promotion relying on shame/disgust and health awareness) and generic NGO/government project delivery and community mobilization, rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access. (Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, plain_criterion2_decision is 'exclude' because the paper also fails Criterion 4.)
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure), and additionally fails Criterion 4. The study investigates factors driving rural communities' social acceptance of behavioral hygiene and sanitation norms promoted by Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) in Burkina Faso. Under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, CLTS social-norm promotion and NGO/government campaign facilitation (institutional pre-triggering meetings, facilitator experience/language, natural leader buy-in, coordination across subsidized vs. unsubsidized NGO campaigns, and motivational visits by officials) constitute behavioural promotion and generic project delivery rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access. Furthermore, although the paper passes the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2 via its 'Governance factors' category, plain_criterion2_decision is also 'exclude' because Criterion 4 is not met: the study reports only respondent citation counts for perceived reasons to accept CLTS behavioral norms (Table 4) and does not measure household sanitation access, latrine ownership/use, availability, affordability, or exclusion.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Target record mismatch leaves the 2000 thesis/report unclear. Evaluated on the retrieved 2004 JAWRA text alone: under the PLAIN wording of Criterion 2, it would pass (plain=yes) because it examines the economic inefficiency of institutional arrangements for surface and ground water management (de facto open access and unenforced deep-well quotas) and models aggregate vs. commercial/industrial ground water pumping quotas alongside PAM Jaya capital investment options (though the 2004 paper would still fail Criterion 3 for lack of empirical evidence, so plain_criterion2_decision on the 2004 paper alone would still be exclude). Under the NARROW 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, the 2004 paper fails (narrow=no) because its modelled policy scenarios concern regional aquifer extraction caps (particularly commercial/industrial pumping quotas) and generic utility capital stock investment rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community water service access (such as connection eligibility, tenure/documentation rules, household tariff/cost-recovery rules, or disconnection/enforcement governing household access), with institutional permitting described only as unanalysed background. Because the 2000 target text itself was not retrieved, overall plain_criterion2_decision is cannot_tell.
rationale: WRONG_PAPER_MISMATCH (paper_mention_mismatch): The Record Metadata identifies Yusman Syaukat's single-authored 2000 work 'Economics of integrated surface and ground water use management in the Jakarta region, Indonesia', whereas the retrieved PDF is a different publication—a 2004 co-authored journal article by Yusman Syaukat and Glenn C. Fox titled 'Conjunctive Surface and Ground Water Management in the Jakarta Region, Indonesia' in JAWRA 40(1):241-250—which explicitly cites 'Y. Syaukat (2000, unpublished Ph.D. thesis, University of Guelph, Canada)' as a separate work (PDF Pages 4 and 6) and acknowledges an EEPSEA Doctoral Fieldwork Research Award (PDF Page 10). Because the 2000 thesis/report itself is not present, we cannot verify without guessing whether it contained primary empirical household fieldwork/survey analyses of water service access absent from this 10-page 2004 optimization paper. (Note: if evaluated solely on the retrieved 2004 JAWRA article, it would be excluded because it is an ex-ante GAMS nonlinear mathematical programming simulation of regional aquifer pumping quotas and aggregate utility investment rather than an empirical evaluation of a rule-type mechanism governing household water service access.)

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper passes Criterion 2 because the field study examines utility tariff structure (variable volumetric metered charges vs. fixed property-value-based charges following a national metering trial), which is a regulatory/institutional pricing factor (alongside psychological community identification). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 fails: although variable versus fixed utility billing is a tariff rule in form, here it does not directly govern service access (eligibility, connection, affordability, continuity, or disconnection), and is instead analyzed strictly as a behavioral financial incentive moderated by psychological community identification to curb discretionary summer water overuse (conservation) among affluent connected households. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the overall full-text decision remains exclude (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because Criteria 1 and 4 are not met.
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; aligns with Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). Van Vugt (2001) is a social-psychological study of common-pool natural resource conservation, testing whether psychological community identification moderates financial incentives (variable metered vs. fixed property-value tariffs) in curbing summer water overuse among already-connected households in an affluent UK town, paired with a student laboratory point-harvesting game. It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access, eligibility, connection, affordability, reliability, basic water sufficiency, or disconnection. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the comparison of utility tariff systems satisfies Criterion 2, whereas under the 2026-10-13 narrow reading the tariff variable is studied as a conservation incentive rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access; under both readings the full-text decision is exclude because Criteria 1 and 4 are not satisfied.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: No under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type mechanism reading (borderline/yes on the literal plain wording, though still excluded overall on C1/C4). Plain wording reading: Under the broad literal wording ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the study arguably touches regulatory and institutional variables because its regression includes Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) primary MCL violation counts, non-mandatory secondary SMCL exceedance percentages, and water-system dummy variables ('Private system', 'Municipal system'), alongside narrative discussion of SMCL regulatory thresholds. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Fails Criterion 2 because none of the analyzed exposures is a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access. Primary MCL violations and SMCL exceedances are used strictly as proxies for physical and aesthetic (taste, odor, color) water contamination driving consumer perception; 'Private system' and 'Municipal system' are unanalyzed background control dummies in Table 2 (never discussed in the prose) regressed against commercial retail store counts rather than utility ownership rules governing household service access; and 'Foreign-born non-citizen' tract share is an ACS demographic indicator used to proxy cultural/home-country tap-water mistrust rather than citizenship or documentation eligibility rules. (Even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains 'exclude' because C1 and C4 are not met.)
rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome; also fails C1 and narrow C2). This empirical spatial econometric study models the per-capita count of commercial retail water stores across 7,020 urbanized California census tracts already served by community water systems as an ecological proxy for consumer tap-water mistrust and avoidance. It does not report an outcome measuring household or community water service access, connection, utility service availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (failing C1 and C4). In addition, under the 2026-10-13 narrow reading of Criterion 2, it does not examine a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism governing service access: SDWA primary MCL violations and secondary SMCL exceedances are used as proxies for physical/organoleptic water contamination affecting consumer perception, private/municipal system dummies are unanalyzed background covariates in Table 2, and foreign-born non-citizen share reflects immigrant home-country perception rather than legal/documentation eligibility rules. Even under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded because it lacks a service-access outcome.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Unclear under both the plain wording of Criterion 2 (any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor) and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, enforcement or utility ownership/regulatory structure directly governing service access), because the full text is not accessible and cannot be inspected.
rationale: reason: "full text not accessible". Retrieval status is not_accessible and no verified full-text PDF, OA XML or abstract text was retrieved for assessment; per screening protocol rules, eligibility cannot be guessed from title/metadata alone, requiring decision "cannot_tell" and exclusion_code "NONE" under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type Criterion 2 reading and the plain Criterion 2 reading.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, it examines financing, institutional support, and governance arrangements for rural water services. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it specifically addresses tariff-setting and cost-recovery rules, payment collection rules (reactive financing, monthly household tariffs, pay-as-you-fetch), community cross-subsidy exemptions, and targeted government subsidy structures governing rural water access and affordability.
